articles.title: 15-second video and lower pricing
articles.text:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings 15-second clips, stronger consistency, and faster, more cost-effective generation.

We’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, which offers native 15-second video creation, improved reference adherence, and multi-turn conversational editing. This update lowers costs by 30% and provides better consistency for your professional projects. You can start using these capabilities today across the Gemini API, Google Vids, and Gemini for business to produce high-quality video content at scale.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

We are launching Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with support for fifteen-second videos and improved reference adherence.
You can now edit clips through multi-turn conversations, which allows for faster adjustments without starting over.
We reduced the price by 30% to help you produce high-quality video content at a lower cost.
This model is generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud for your production needs.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.Here’s an overview of what’s new:Fast and cost-effective at scaleBeyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.Longer clips up to 15 secondsYou can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.Better reference adherenceYou can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.

Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.

More consistent resultsYou can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.

Easier editing in conversationYou can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.

Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.

More natural speechYou can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.

Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.

More controllable, cinematic lookYou can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.

Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.

Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistencyGemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.

Real-world results, from creatives to global brands

Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 FlashWhile development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic IPO valuation talks drop to $1.3T
articles.title: Anthropic IPO Valuation Talks Drop to $1.3 Trillion as Major Investors Balk at $1.5T Target — epyhia.com
articles.text:
Anthropic's planned initial public offering — which could be the first for a frontier AI model developer — is being repriced in real time. Prospective investors are now discussing a valuation of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, down from the $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion range communicated to bankers just days earlier, and far below the $2 trillion figures floated in early October, Bloomberg reported Friday according to Investing.com [1]. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that three major prospective investors said the offering would need to be priced lower, with one suggesting a valuation closer to $1 trillion [1].
The reassessment follows Thursday's 6.4% plunge in the Nasdaq 100, which wiped out roughly $2.3 trillion in market value in its largest single-day decline on record [1]. The Cboe Volatility Index climbed to its highest level since April 2025 [1].
Valuation trajectory: $2T → $1.5T → $1.3T
Anthropic's valuation expectations have retreated in three steps. Early October discussions reached $2 trillion. After an investor briefing on financial performance, the range fell to $1.4–1.5 trillion. Thursday's market rout prompted the latest downward revision to $1.2–1.3 trillion [1]. Bloomberg's reporting suggests investors and bankers are still working toward an offering rather than abandoning the timetable [1].
Anthropic declined to comment on the valuation discussions [1][3].
Financials: explosive revenue, accounting-driven losses, massive compute commitments
The company's amended S-1 filing reveals the scale of both the opportunity and the capital intensity [2][6]:
Revenue: $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12× year-over-year. Nine-month revenue: $33.24 billion. Annualized run rate: ~$68 billion.Net loss: $23.3 billion in Q3; $104 billion for the first nine months. The filing shows 90% of the first-half loss ($72.4 billion of $80.5 billion) came from fair-value remeasurement of convertible notes — primarily from Amazon — whose carrying value rises as Anthropic's valuation climbs. This accounting effect largely disappears after the IPO when notes convert to equity [2].Operating performance: Roughly break-even in Q3 ($17.5B operating expenses vs. $17B revenue). Q2 showed ~$974 million operating profit. Operating cash flow was positive $3.9 billion in the first half; reports suggest free cash flow turned positive in Q3. Gross margin ~85% [2].Compute commitments: $895.4 billion in purchase and lease agreements, "substantially all" for compute and infrastructure. ~$447.5 billion due by end of 2030; ~$69.8 billion due in the 12 months after September 30, 2026 [2][6]. That near-term obligation is roughly four times current quarterly revenue.
The commitments explain why Anthropic needs to raise capital at scale. The IPO, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley with 20 other banks, aims to raise at least as much as SpaceX's record $86.2 billion debut. The stock would trade on Nasdaq under ticker ANT [2].
METR finds 2× faster model improvement, driven by AI-assisted research
An independent evaluation by Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), given "unprecedented access to internal data" over roughly 11 weeks (mid-August through late October), estimated Anthropic is improving model capabilities on "well-specified tasks" around twice as fast as a year ago [4]. METR said it was able to "confidently" rule out compute growth as the driver, and said its guess was that the acceleration came from AI systems helping develop newer AI systems — the "closing the loop" dynamic Anthropic describes in its filing [4][6].
Caveats are significant. METR said the acceleration might be limited to tasks that can be graded automatically, not "messy" real-world tasks. It could also reflect understatement of prior progress. Internal disagreements and uncertainty among METR's team were noted [4]. Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment on the report [4].
CEO Dario Amodei publicly called for the industry to "slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models" in a September 12 essay, warning that recursive self-improvement could "outrun our ability to understand and control these systems" [4]. Amodei championed METR as an appropriate third-party evaluator; OpenAI's Sam Altman also supported the idea [4].
IPO timing uncertain: roadshow, October revenue, political headwinds
Reuters reported the roadshow was expected to kick off the week of November 9, with pricing the following week [3]. But four people familiar with investor discussions said potential investors are raising doubts about whether Anthropic can proceed on that timeline [3]. Investors are pushing for a more attractive valuation and are eagerly awaiting Anthropic's October revenue figure, which the company left blank in its updated S-1 [3].
A delay would amplify concerns about the AI ecosystem's health, particularly as ballot measures in multiple states limiting data center development have crystallized political opposition to AI infrastructure [3]. Microsoft tightened oversight of some data center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, Bloomberg reported Thursday; Nebius, Iren, and CoreWeave have each lost roughly half their value over the past month [3]. CoreWeave and SpaceX credit default swaps hit records implying rising default expectations [3].
Tech stocks have underperformed the S&P 500 by 10.7% over the past month — the most extreme one-month underperformance since May 2002, according to Truist Advisory Services [3]. Vanda Research said retail selling was the strongest since the COVID-19 pandemic [3].
What remains unknown
Whether Anthropic proceeds at a $1.2–1.3T valuation, seeks a smaller raise, or delays past Thanksgiving.October revenue — a key data point investors are waiting for.How much of the $895.4B in commitments is firm versus contingent, and whether public-market investors will fund a capital plan that extends to 2045.Whether the "closing the loop" acceleration METR observed translates to broader capabilities or remains confined to benchmarkable tasks.
The distinction between a repricing and a postponement matters. If Anthropic goes public at a "more grounded valuation," it would test whether demand for leading AI businesses survives a sector correction [1]. For now, the company that says it wants to slow down is being forced to speed up its pitch to public markets.

articles.sourceTitle: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
articles.title: Mark Cuban says Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads as Meta docs reveal $16 billion in fraud-linked revenue
articles.text: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images/Finn Gomez/Getty Images           Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.          "Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.              Must Read            Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one         Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP         A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change            Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."          The ads Cuban says Meta waves through          Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.              "The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.          Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.          What Meta's documents showed          On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.          In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.               Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.              Meanwhile, Meta's newest AI product has been causing headaches of its own. A Toronto man let the company's AI agent run his Facebook Marketplace listings on Sept. 26, and it gave a buyer his street address and said yes to a lowball offer. He later traced part of the problem to a permission setting he'd picked.         Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors         Why older adults keep paying the price         Older Americans lose more to this kind of crime than any other age group. People 60 and older told the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center they lost $7.7 billion in 2025, across 201,266 complaints — 59% more money than the year before, according to the bureau's 2025 Internet Crime Report. Investment schemes did the worst damage at $3.5 billion, with tech and customer support scams taking another $1.04 billion.            AI showed up in more than 3,100 of those complaints, and together those victims lost over $352 million. That's only counting the people who spoke up — plenty never file at all.         How to protect yourself — and your parents         Anytime you see a famous face advertising something pop up in your feed, assume it's fake — Cuban himself included in that. Run the product's name through a search with the word "scam" next to it. Then think about who in your family is on Facebook the most – and send them a message warning them about it.         And if you suspect anything fishy, file a report the same day to the Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. The FBI froze $32.9 million worth of funds tied to older victims' cases in 2025, the agency says, but it can only chase money it knows about.         Moneywise reached out to Meta for comment on Cuban's reply but did not immediately receive a response. I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
articles.title: Arjun Panickssery's Shortform — LessWrong
articles.text:
I struggle to believe at an intuitive level that autonomous R&D is so ingenious. I have been monitoring a few side projects:

Building a new SOTA engine for Scrabble (current SOTA is not really a neural-network method and doesn't beat the strongest human player)
Building a bot to play Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe
Researching philosophy and formalizing some proofs for the AI Philosophy contest

In all of these cases, the model's judgment is just very poor in a basic way. For example:

When reviewing literature, it fails to identify the specific papers or blog posts that are obviously the most important and useful.
It will conduct experiments that have no information value because the amount of training data used was obviously too small to distinguish the architectures to be compared.
In the philosophy project, where it built a wiki over many tokens and investigations, it kept going down directions which were extremely trivial and had little value.
For Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, I saw a very clever idea in a blog post that I doubt Astra would ever have come up with; it actually located the blog post but didn't realize its importance or relevance (which could be discerned easily from his strong performance in an online arena and the recency of the post) over papers from previous years that are obviously less relevant.

I judged an Apart hackathon last weekend and reviewed eight papers, all of which scored between 60% and 95% on Pangram. Predictably, the papers were often very similar to each other, and kind of methodologically incomplete in a vague but similar way, where they seem to overlook the most straightforward analysis.

Maybe the important exception is certain hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops. For example, I improved the SOTA on "listing all legal Scrabble moves" by 10x just by prompting Astra over and over to try harder, to aim for <specific performance level>, to "systematically try every method in the literature that seems kind of related," etc. But even in that case, two big leaps were when I said that it should take into account the fact that you can measure across a game rather than per random position, and suggesting that it try to design algorithms for three different cases based on the number of blank tiles left in the bag (which cause the number of moves to explode).

There is also the fact that Astra at least (and presumably Claude) tends to write reports that are extremely difficult to understand and some kind of Q&A interrogation is often needed to figure out what it actually did and what the key results are. Maybe there's a temptation to just say "whatever" and let it rip.
